{{Short description|Automaton which either accepts or rejects infinite inputs}}
[[File:2-state Buchi automaton.svg|thumb|alt=A Büchi automaton|A Büchi automaton with two states, <math>q_0</math> and <math>q_1</math>, the former of which is the start state and the latter of which is accepting. Its inputs are infinite words over the symbols <math>\{a,b\}</math>. As an example, it accepts the infinite word <math>(ab)^\omega</math>, where <math>x^\omega</math> denotes the infinite repetition of a string <math>x</math>. It rejects the infinite word <math>aaab^\omega</math>.]]
In [[computer science]] and [[automata theory]], a '''deterministic Büchi automaton''' is a theoretical machine which either accepts or rejects infinite inputs. Such a machine has a set of states and a transition function, which determines which state the machine should move to from its current state when it reads the next input character. Some states are accepting states and one state is the start state. The machine accepts an input [[if and only if]] it will pass through an accepting state infinitely many times as it reads the input.

A '''non-deterministic Büchi automaton''', later referred to just as a '''Büchi automaton''', has a transition function which may have multiple outputs, leading to many possible paths for the same input; it accepts an infinite input if and only if some possible path is accepting. Deterministic and non-deterministic Büchi automata generalize [[deterministic finite automaton|deterministic finite automata]] and [[nondeterministic finite automaton|nondeterministic finite automata]] to infinite inputs. Each are types of [[ω-automaton|ω-automata]]. Büchi automata recognize the [[Omega-regular language|ω-regular languages]], the infinite word version of [[regular language]]s. They are named after the Swiss mathematician [[Julius Richard Büchi]], who invented them in 1962.<ref name=":0">{{cite book | first = J.R. | last = Büchi | title = The Collected Works of J. Richard Büchi | chapter = On a Decision Method in Restricted Second Order Arithmetic | journal = Proc. International Congress on Logic, Method, and Philosophy of Science. 1960 | pages = 425–435 | location = Stanford | date = 1962 | publisher = Stanford University Press | doi = 10.1007/978-1-4613-8928-6_23 | isbn = 978-1-4613-8930-9 }}</ref>

Büchi automata are often used in [[model checking]] as an automata-theoretic version of a formula in [[linear temporal logic]].

== Formal definition ==
Formally, a '''deterministic Büchi automaton''' is a tuple {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, \mathbf{F})</math>}} that consists of the following components:

* {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q</math>}} is a [[finite set]]. The elements of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q</math>}} are called the ''states'' of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}}.
* {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Sigma</math>}} is a finite set called the ''alphabet'' of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}}.
* {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \delta \colon Q \times \Sigma \to Q</math>}} is a function, called the ''transition function'' of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}}.
* {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> q_0</math>}} is an element of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q</math>}}, called the ''initial state'' of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}}.
* {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \mathbf{F} \subseteq Q</math>}} is the ''acceptance condition''.

A '''run''' <math>\underline{i} = i_0i_1i_2 \cdots \in \Sigma^\omega</math> is an infinite string of inputs of <math>A</math>.
By calling <math>\delta</math> recursively, we can extend it to a function <math>\delta^\omega : \Sigma^\omega \to Q^\omega </math>.
A state <math>q \in Q</math> is said to ''occur infinitely often'' for a run <math>\underline{i}</math> when the set <math>\{n \in \N \mid \delta^\omega(\underline{i})_n = q\}</math> is infinite. Let <math>\mathrm{Inf}(\underline{i})</math> be the set of states occurring infinitely often for <math>\underline{i}</math>. The '''language of <math>A</math>''' is then the set of runs of <math>A</math> in which at least one of the infinitely-often occurring states is in {{nowrap|<math display="inline">\mathbf{F}</math>}}; in symbols:
<math display="block">L(A) = \{ \underline{i} \in \Sigma^\omega \mid \mathrm{Inf}(\underline{i}) \cap \mathbf{F} \neq \varnothing \}.</math>

In a ('''non-deterministic''') '''Büchi automaton''', the transition function {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \delta</math>}} is replaced with a transition relation {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Delta</math>}} that returns a set of states, and the single initial state {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> q_0</math>}} is replaced by a set {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> I</math>}} of initial states. Generally, the term Büchi automaton without qualifier refers to non-deterministic Büchi automata.

For more comprehensive formalism see also [[ω-automaton]].

== Closure properties ==
The set of Büchi automata is [[closed under]] the following operations.

Let <math> A=(Q_A,\Sigma,\Delta_A,I_A,{F}_A)</math> and <math> B=(Q_B,\Sigma,\Delta_B,I_B,{F}_B)</math> be Büchi automata and <math> C=(Q_C,\Sigma,\Delta_C,I_C,{F}_C)</math>  be a [[finite automaton]].

* '''Union''': ''There is a Büchi automaton that recognizes the language <math> L(A)\cup L(B).</math>''
: '''Proof:''' If we assume, ''[[w.l.o.g.]]'', <math> Q_A\cap Q_B</math> is empty then <math> L(A)\cup L(B)</math> is recognized by the Büchi automaton <math> (Q_A\cup Q_B, \Sigma\cup \Sigma, \Delta_A\cup \Delta_B, I_A\cup I_B, {F}_A\cup {F}_B).</math>
* '''Intersection''': ''There is a Büchi automaton that recognizes the language <math> L(A)\cap L(B).</math>''
: '''Proof:''' The Büchi automaton <math> A'=(Q',\Sigma,\Delta',I',F')</math> recognizes <math> L(A)\cap L(B),</math> where
:* <math> Q' = Q_A \times Q_B \times \{1,2\}</math>
:* <math> \Delta' = \Delta_1 \cup  \Delta_2</math>
:** <math> \Delta_1 = \{( (q_A,q_B,1), a, (q'_A,q'_B,i) ) | (q_A,a,q'_A)\in \Delta_A\text{ and }(q_B,a,q'_B)\in \Delta_B\text{ and if }q_A\in F_A\text{ then }i=2\text{ else }i=1 \}</math>
:** <math> \Delta_2 = \{( (q_A,q_B,2), a, (q'_A,q'_B,i) ) | (q_A,a,q'_A)\in \Delta_A\text{ and }(q_B,a,q'_B)\in \Delta_B\text{ and if }q_B\in F_B\text{ then }i=1\text{ else }i=2 \}</math>
:* <math> I' = I_A \times I_B \times \{1\}</math>
:* <math> F' = \{ (q_A,q_B,2) | q_B\in F_B \}</math>
: By construction, <math> r'=(q_A^0,q_B^0,i^0),(q_A^1,q_B^1,i^1),\dots</math> is a run of automaton A' on input word {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w</math>}} if <math> r_A=q_A^0,q_A^1,\dots</math> is run of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} on {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w</math>}} and <math> r_B=q_B^0,q_B^1,\dots</math> is run of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> B</math>}} on {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w</math>}}. {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> r_A</math>}} is accepting and {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> r_B</math>}} is accepting if {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> r'</math>}} is concatenation of an infinite series of finite segments of 1-states (states with third component 1) and 2-states (states with third component 2) alternatively. There is such a series of segments of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> r'</math>}} if {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> r'</math>}} is accepted by {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A'</math>}}.
* '''Concatenation''': ''There is a Büchi automaton that recognizes the language <math> L(C) \cdot L(A).</math>''
: '''Proof:''' If we assume, ''w.l.o.g.'', <math> Q_C\cap Q_A</math> is empty then the Büchi automaton <math> A'=(Q_C\cup Q_A,\Sigma,\Delta',I',F_A)</math> recognizes <math> L(C)\cdot L(A)</math>, where
:* <math> \Delta' = \Delta_A \cup  \Delta_C \cup  \{ (q,a,q') | q'\in I_A\text{ and }\exists f\in F_C. (q,a,f)\in \Delta_C \}</math>
:* <math> \text{ if }I_C\cap F_C\text{ is empty then }I' = I_C\text{ otherwise }I' = I_C \cup I_A</math>
* '''&omega;-closure''': ''If <math> L(C)</math> does not contain the empty word then there is a Büchi automaton that recognizes the language <math> L(C)^\omega.</math>''
: '''Proof:''' The Büchi automaton that recognizes <math> L(C)^\omega</math> is constructed in two stages. First, we construct a finite automaton {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A'</math>}} such that {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A'</math>}} also recognizes <math> L(C)</math> but there are no incoming transitions to initial states of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A'</math>}}. So, <math> A'=(Q_C \cup  \{q_\text{new}\},\Sigma,\Delta',\{q_\text{new}\},F_C),</math> where <math> \Delta' = \Delta_C \cup  \{ (q_\text{new},a,q') | \exists q\in I_C. (q,a,q')\in \Delta_C\}.</math> Note that <math> L(C)=L(A')</math> because <math> L(C)</math> does not contain the empty string. Second, we will construct the Büchi automaton {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A''</math>}} that recognize <math> L(C)^\omega</math> by adding a loop back to the initial state of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A'</math>}}. So, <math> A''=(Q_C \cup  \{q_\text{new}\},\Sigma,\Delta'',\{q_\text{new}\},\{q_\text{new}\})</math>, where <math> \Delta'' = \Delta' \cup  \{ (q,a,q_\text{new}) | \exists q'\in F_C. (q,a,q')\in \Delta'\}.</math>
* '''Complementation''':''There is a Büchi automaton that recognizes the language <math> \Sigma^\omega/L(A).</math>''
: '''Proof:''' The proof is presented [[Complementation of Büchi automaton|here]].

== Recognizable languages ==
Büchi automata recognize the [[ω-regular language]]s. Using the definition of ω-regular language and the above closure properties of Büchi automata, it can be easily shown that a Büchi automaton  can be constructed such that it recognizes any given ω-regular language. For converse, see [[ω-regular language#Equivalence to Büchi automaton|construction of a ω-regular language]] for a Büchi automaton.

=== Deterministic versus non-deterministic Büchi automata ===

[[File:Buchi non deterministic example.svg|thumb|200px|A non-deterministic Büchi automaton that recognizes {{tmath|(0\cup 1)^* 0^\omega}}]]

The class of deterministic Büchi automata does not suffice to encompass all omega-regular languages. In particular, there is no deterministic Büchi automaton that recognizes the language {{tmath|(0\cup 1)^* 0^\omega}}, which contains exactly words in which 1 occurs only finitely many times.  We can demonstrate it by contradiction that no such deterministic Büchi automaton exists. Let us suppose {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} is a deterministic Büchi automaton that recognizes {{tmath|(0\cup 1)^* 0^\omega}} with final state set {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \mathbf{F}</math>}}. {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} accepts {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> 0^\omega</math>}}. So, {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} will visit some state in {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \mathbf{F}</math>}} after reading some finite prefix of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> 0^\omega</math>}}, say after the {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> i_0</math>}}th letter. {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} also accepts the ω-word {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> 0^{i_0} 1 0^\omega</math>}}. Therefore, for some {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> i_1</math>}}, after the prefix {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> 0^{i_0} 1 0^{i_1}</math>}} the automaton will visit some state in {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \mathbf{F}</math>}}. Continuing with this construction the ω-word {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> 0^{i_0} 1 0^{i_1} 1 0^{i_2} \dots</math>}} is generated which causes {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} to visit some state in {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \mathbf{F}</math>}} infinitely often and the word is not in {{tmath|(0\cup 1)^* 0^\omega.}} Contradiction.

The class of languages recognizable by deterministic Büchi automata is characterized by the following lemma.

: '''Lemma:''' ''An ω-language is recognizable by a deterministic Büchi automaton if it is the [[Omega language#Operations|limit language]] of some [[regular language]].''
: '''Proof:''' Any deterministic Büchi automaton {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} can be viewed as a deterministic finite automaton {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A'</math>}} and vice versa, since both types of automaton are defined as 5-tuple of the same components, only the interpretation of acceptance condition is different. We will show that {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> L(A)</math>}} is the limit language of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> L(A')</math>}}. An ω-word is accepted by {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} if it will force {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} to visit final states infinitely often. Thus, infinitely many finite prefixes of this ω-word will be accepted by {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A'</math>}}. Hence, {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> L(A)</math>}} is a limit language of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> L(A')</math>}}.

== Algorithms ==
[[Model checking]] of finite state systems can often be translated into various operations on Büchi automata.
In addition to the closure operations presented above,
the following are some useful operations for the applications of Büchi automata.

; Determinization

Since deterministic Büchi automata are strictly less expressive than non-deterministic automata, there can not be an algorithm for determinization of Büchi automata.
But, [[McNaughton's Theorem]] and [[Safra's construction]] provide algorithms that can translate a Büchi automaton into a deterministic [[Muller automaton]] or deterministic [[Rabin automaton]].<ref name=":1">{{citation
 | last = Safra | first = S. | authorlink = Shmuel Safra
 | contribution = On the complexity of ω-automata
 | doi = 10.1109/SFCS.1988.21948
 | location = Washington DC, US
 | pages = 319–327
 | publisher = IEEE Computer Society
 | title = Proceedings of the 29th Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS '88)
 | year = 1988| isbn = 0-8186-0877-3 | s2cid = 206559211 }}.</ref>

; Emptiness checking

The language recognized by a Büchi automaton is non-empty if and only if there is a final state that is both reachable from the initial state, and lies on a cycle.

An effective algorithm that can check emptiness of a Büchi automaton:

# Consider the automaton as a [[directed graph]] and decompose it into [[strongly connected component]]s (SCCs).
# Run a search (e.g., the [[depth-first search]]) to find which SCCs are reachable from the initial state.
# Check whether there is a non-trivial SCC that is reachable and contains a final state.

Each of the steps of this algorithm can be done in time linear in the automaton size, hence the algorithm is clearly optimal.

; Minimization

Minimizing deterministic Büchi automata (i.e., given a deterministic Büchi automaton, finding a deterministic Büchi automaton recognizing the same language with a minimal number of states) is an NP-complete problem.<ref>{{cite arXiv |first=Sven |last=Schewe |title=Minimisation of Deterministic Parity and Büchi Automata and Relative Minimisation of Deterministic Finite Automata |year=2010 |class=cs.FL |eprint=1007.1333 }}</ref> This is in contrast to [[DFA minimization]], which can be done in polynomial time.

== Transforming from other models of description to non-deterministic Büchi automata ==
=== From [[Generalized Büchi automaton|generalized Büchi automata]] (GBA) ===

: Multiple sets of states in acceptance condition can be translated into one set of states by an automata construction, which is known as "counting construction". Let's say {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A = (Q, \Sigma, \Delta, q_0, \{F_1, \ldots, F_n\})</math>}} is a GBA, where {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> F_1, \ldots, F_n</math>}} are sets of accepting states then the equivalent Büchi automaton is {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A' = (Q', \Sigma, \Delta', q'_0, F')</math>}}, where
:* {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q' = Q \times \{1, \ldots, n\}</math>}}
:* {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> q'_0 = (q_0, 1)</math>}}
:* {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Delta' = \{ ((q, i), a, (q', j)) \mid (q, a, q') \in \Delta \text{ and if } q \in F_i \text{ then } j = ((i+1) \bmod n) \text{ else } j = i \}</math>}}
:* {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> F' = F_1 \times \{1\}</math>}}

=== From [[Linear temporal logic]] formula ===
: A translation from a Linear temporal logic formula to a generalized Büchi automaton is given [[Linear temporal logic to Büchi automaton|here]]. And, a translation from a generalized Büchi automaton to a Büchi automaton is presented above.

=== From [[Muller automaton|Muller automata]] ===
: A given Muller automaton can be transformed into an equivalent Büchi automaton with the following automata construction. Let's suppose {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A = (Q, \Sigma, \Delta, Q_0, \{F_0, \ldots, F_n\})</math>}} is a Muller automaton, where {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> F_0, \ldots, F_n</math>}} are sets of accepting states. An equivalent Büchi automaton is {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A' = (Q', \Sigma, \Delta', Q_0, F')</math>}}, where
:* {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q' = Q \cup \bigcup_{i=0}^{n} \{i\} \times F_i \times 2^{F_i}</math>}}
:* {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Delta' = \Delta \cup \Delta_1 \cup \Delta_2</math>}}, where
:** {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Delta_1 = \{ (q, a, (i, q', \emptyset)) \mid (q, a, q') \in \Delta \text{ and } q' \in F_i \}</math>}}
:** {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Delta_2 = \{ ((i, q, R), a, (i, q', R')) \mid (q, a, q') \in \Delta \text{ and } q, q' \in F_i \text{ and if } R = F_i \text{ then } R' = \emptyset \text{ otherwise } R' = R \cup \{q\} \}</math>}}
:* {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> F' = \bigcup_{i=0}^{n} \{i\} \times F_i \times \{F_i\}</math>}}
: {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A'</math>}} keeps original set of states from {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} and adds extra states on them. The Büchi automaton {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A'</math>}} simulates the Muller automaton {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} as follows: At the beginning of the input word, the execution of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A'</math>}} follows the execution of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}}, since initial states are same and {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Delta'</math>}} contains {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Delta</math>}}. At some non-deterministically chosen position in the input word, {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A'</math>}} decides of jump into newly added states via a transition in {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Delta_1</math>}}. Then, the transitions in {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Delta_2</math>}} try to visit all the states of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> F_i</math>}} and keep growing {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> R</math>}}. Once {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> R</math>}} becomes equal to {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> F_i</math>}} then it is reset to the [[empty set]] and {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Delta_2</math>}} try to visit all the states of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> F_i</math>}} states again and again. So, if the states {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> R = F_i</math>}} are visited infinitely often then {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A'</math>}} accepts corresponding input and so does {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}}. This construction closely follows the first part of the proof of [[McNaughton's Theorem]].

=== From Kripke structures ===
: Let the given [[Kripke structure]] be defined by {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> M = \langle Q, I, R, L, AP \rangle</math>}} where {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q</math>}} is the set of states, {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> I</math>}} is the set of initial states, {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> R</math>}} is a relation between two states also interpreted as an edge, {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> L</math>}} is the label for the state and {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> AP</math>}} are the set of atomic propositions that form {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> L</math>}}.

: The Büchi automaton will have the following characteristics:
:: <math>Q_\text{final} = Q \cup \{ \text{init} \}</math>
:: <math>\Sigma = 2^{AP}</math>
:: <math>I =\{ \text{init} \}</math>
:: <math>F = Q \cup \{ \text{init} \}</math>
:: <math>\delta = q \overrightarrow{a} p </math> if {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> (q, p)</math>}} belongs to {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> R</math>}} and {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> L(p) = a</math>}}

: and {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \text{init} \overrightarrow{a} q</math>}} if {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> q</math>}} belongs to {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> I</math>}} and {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> L(q) = a</math>}}.

: Note however that there is a difference in the interpretation between Kripke structures and Büchi automata. While the former explicitly names every state variable's polarity for every state, the latter just declares the current set of variables holding or not holding true. It says absolutely nothing about the other variables that could be present in the model.

==Complementation==
In [[automata theory]], '''complementation of a Büchi automaton''' is the task of [[complementation of automata|complementing]] a Büchi automaton, i.e., constructing another automaton that recognizes the complement of the [[ω-regular language]] recognized by the given Büchi automaton. Existence of algorithms for this construction proves that the set of ω-regular languages is [[closed under]] complementation.

This construction is particularly hard relative to the constructions for the other [[Büchi automaton#Closure properties|closure properties of Büchi automata]]. The first construction was presented by Büchi in 1962.<ref name=":0" /> Later, other constructions were developed that enabled efficient and optimal complementation.<ref>{{citation|last=McNaughton|first=R.|authorlink = Robert McNaughton|title=Testing and generating infinite sequences by a finite automaton|journal=[[Information and Control]]|volume=9|pages=521–530|year=1966|issue=5 |doi=10.1016/s0019-9958(66)80013-x|doi-access=free}}.</ref><ref>{{citation|first1=A. P.|last1=Sistla|first2=M. Y.|last2=Vardi|author2-link=Moshe Vardi|first3=P.|last3=Wolper|author3-link=Pierre Wolper|title=The complementation problem for Büchi automata with applications to temporal logic|journal=[[Theoretical Computer Science (journal)|Theoretical Computer Science]]|volume=49|pages=217–237|year=1987|issue=2–3 |doi=10.1016/0304-3975(87)90008-9|doi-access=free}}.</ref><ref name=":1" /><ref>{{citation|first1=O.|last1=Kupferman|author1link = Orna Kupferman|first2=M. Y.|last2=Vardi|author2-link=Moshe Vardi|title= Weak alternating automata are not that weak|journal=[[ACM Transactions on Computational Logic]]|volume=2|issue=3|pages=408–429|date=July 2001|doi=10.1145/377978.377993 }}.</ref><ref>{{ cite conference |url=https://inria.hal.science/inria-00360108/document |title=Büchi Complementation Made Tight |first=Sven |last=Schewe |date=2009 |conference=STACS}}</ref>

===Büchi's construction===
Büchi presented<ref name=":0" /> a doubly exponential complement construction  in a logical form. Here, we have his construction in the modern notation used in automata theory.
Let {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A = (Q, \Sigma, \Delta, Q_0, \mathbf{F})</math>}} be a Büchi automaton.
Let {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \sim_A</math>}} be an [[equivalence relation]] over elements of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Sigma^+</math>}} such that
for each {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> v, w \in \Sigma^+</math>}},
{{nowrap|<math display="inline"> v \sim_A w</math>}} if and only if for all {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> p, q \in Q</math>}},
{{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} has a run from {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> p</math>}} to {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> q</math>}} over {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> v</math>}} if and only if this is possible over {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w</math>}}
and furthermore
{{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} has a run via {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \mathbf{F}</math>}} from {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> p</math>}} to {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> q</math>}} over {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> v</math>}} if and only if this is possible over {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w</math>}}.
Each class of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \sim_A</math>}} defines a map {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> f \colon Q \to 2^Q \times 2^Q</math>}}
in the following way:
for each state {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> p \in Q</math>}}, we have {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> (Q_1, Q_2) = f(p)</math>}}, where
{{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q_1 = \{q \in Q \mid w \text{ can move automaton } A \text{ from } p \text{ to } q\}</math>}} and {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q_2 = \{q \in Q \mid w \text{ can move automaton } A \text{ from } p \text{ to } q \text{ via a state in } \mathbf{F}\}</math>}}.
Note that {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q_2 \subseteq Q_1</math>}}.
If {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> f</math>}} is a map definable in this way, we denote the (unique) class defining {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> f</math>}} by {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> L_f</math>}}.

The following three theorems provide a construction of the complement of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}}
using the [[equivalence classes]] of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \sim_A</math>}}.

'''Theorem 1:''' {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \sim_A</math>}} has finitely many equivalent classes and each class is a [[regular language]].<br>
'''Proof:'''
Since there are finitely many {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> f \colon Q \to 2^Q \times 2^Q</math>}}, the relation {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \sim_A</math>}} has finitely many equivalence classes.
Now we show that {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> L_f</math>}} is a regular language.
For {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> p, q \in Q</math>}} and {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> i \in \{0, 1\}</math>}},
let {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A_{i,p,q} = (\{0,1\} \times Q, \; \Sigma, \; \Delta_1 \cup \Delta_2, \; \{(0, p)\}, \; \{(i, q)\})</math>}}
be a [[nondeterministic finite automaton]],
where
{{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Delta_1 = \{ ((0, q_1), (0, q_2)) \mid (q_1, q_2) \in \Delta \} \cup \{ ((1, q_1), (1, q_2)) \mid (q_1, q_2) \in \Delta \}</math>}},
and
{{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Delta_2 = \{ ((0, q_1), (1, q_2)) \mid q_1 \in \mathbf{F} \land (q_1, q_2) \in \Delta \}</math>}}.
Let {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q' \subseteq Q</math>}}.
Let {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \alpha_{p, Q'} = \bigcap \{ L(A_{1, p, q}) \mid q \in Q' \}</math>}},
which is the set of words that can move {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} from {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> p</math>}} to all the states in {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q'</math>}}
via some state in {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \mathbf{F}</math>}}.
Let {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \beta_{p, Q'} = \bigcap \{ L(A_{0, p, q}) - L(A_{1, p, q}) - \{\varepsilon\} \mid q \in Q' \}</math>}},
which is the set of non-empty words that can move {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} from {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> p</math>}} to all the states in {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q'</math>}}
and does not have a run that passes through any state in {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \mathbf{F}</math>}}.
Let {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \gamma_{p, Q'} = \bigcap \{ \Sigma^+ - L(A_{0, p, q}) \mid q \in Q' \}</math>}},
which is the set of non-empty words that cannot move {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} from {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> p</math>}} to any of the
states in {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q'</math>}}. Since the regular languages are closed under finite intersections and under relative complements, every {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \alpha_{p, Q'}</math>}}, {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \beta_{p, Q'}</math>}}, and {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \gamma_{p, Q'}</math>}} is regular.
By definitions,
{{nowrap|<math display="inline"> L_f = \bigcap \{ \alpha_{p, Q_2} \cap \beta_{p, Q_1 - Q_2} \cap \gamma_{p, Q - Q_1} \mid (Q_1, Q_2) = f(p) \land p \in Q \}</math>}}.

'''Theorem 2:''' For each {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w \in \Sigma^\omega</math>}},
there are {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \sim_A</math>}} classes {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> L_f</math>}} and {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> L_g</math>}} such that
{{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w \in L_f (L_g)^\omega</math>}}.
<br>
'''Proof:'''
We will use the [[Ramsey's Theorem#Infinite Ramsey theorem|infinite Ramsey theorem]]
to prove this theorem.
Let {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w = a_0 a_1 \ldots</math>}} and {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w(i, j) = a_i \ldots a_{j-1}</math>}}.
Consider the set of natural numbers {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \mathbb{N}</math>}}.
Let equivalence classes of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \sim_A</math>}} be the colors of subsets of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \mathbb{N}</math>}}
of size 2.
We assign the colors as follows.
For each {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> i < j</math>}},
let the color of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \{i, j\}</math>}} be the equivalence class in which {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w(i, j)</math>}} occurs.
By the infinite Ramsey theorem, we can find an [[infinite set]] {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> X \subseteq \mathbb{N}</math>}}
such that each subset of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> X</math>}} of size 2 has same color.
Let {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> 0 < i_0 < i_1 < i_2 \ldots \in X</math>}}.
Let {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> f</math>}} be a defining map of an equivalence class such that
{{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w(0, i_0) \in L_f</math>}}.
Let {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> g</math>}} be a defining map of an equivalence class such that
for each {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> j > 0</math>}}, {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w(i_{j-1}, i_j) \in L_g</math>}}.
Then {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w \in L_f (L_g)^\omega</math>}}.

'''Theorem 3:'''  Let {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> L_f</math>}} and {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> L_g</math>}} be equivalence classes
of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \sim_A</math>}}.
Then {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> L_f (L_g)^\omega</math>}} is either a subset of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> L(A)</math>}} or
disjoint from {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> L(A)</math>}}. <br>
'''Proof:'''
Suppose there is a word {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w \in L(A) \cap L_f (L_g)^\omega</math>}}, otherwise the theorem holds trivially.
Let {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> r</math>}} be an accepting run of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} over input {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w</math>}}.
We need to show that each word {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w' \in L_f (L_g)^\omega</math>}}
is also in {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> L(A)</math>}}, i.e., there exists a run {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> r'</math>}} of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} over input {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w'</math>}} such that
a state in {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \mathbf{F}</math>}} occurs in {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> r'</math>}} infinitely often.
Since {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w \in L_f (L_g)^\omega</math>}},
let {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w_0 w_1 w_2 \ldots = w</math>}} such that {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w_0 \in L_f</math>}} and for each {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> i > 0</math>}}, {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w_i \in L_g</math>}}.
Let {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> s_i</math>}} be the state in {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> r</math>}} after consuming {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w_0 \ldots w_i</math>}}.
Let {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> I</math>}} be a set of indices such that {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> i \in I</math>}} if and only if the run segment in {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> r</math>}}
from {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> s_i</math>}} to {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> s_{i+1}</math>}} contains a state from {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \mathbf{F}</math>}}.
{{nowrap|<math display="inline"> I</math>}} must be an infinite set.
Similarly, we can split the word {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w'</math>}}.
Let {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w'_0 w'_1 w'_2 \ldots = w'</math>}} such that {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w'_0 \in L_f</math>}} and for each {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> i > 0</math>}}, {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w'_i \in L_g</math>}}.
We construct {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> r'</math>}} inductively in the following way.
Let the first state of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> r'</math>}} be same as {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> r</math>}}. By definition of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> L_f</math>}},
we can choose a run segment on word {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w'_0</math>}} to reach {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> s_0</math>}}.
By induction hypothesis,
we have a run on {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w'_0 \ldots w'_i</math>}} that reaches to {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> s_i</math>}}.
By definition of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> L_g</math>}},
we can extend the run along the word segment {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w'_{i+1}</math>}} such that
the extension reaches {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> s_{i+1}</math>}} and visits a state in {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \mathbf{F}</math>}} if {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> i \in I</math>}}.
The {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> r'</math>}} obtained from this process will have infinitely many run segments
containing states from {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \mathbf{F}</math>}}, since {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> I</math>}} is infinite.
Therefore, {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> r'</math>}} is an accepting run and {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> w' \in L(A)</math>}}.

By the above theorems, we can represent {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Sigma^\omega - L(A)</math>}}
as finite union of [[ω-regular language]]s of the form {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> L_f (L_g)^\omega</math>}}, where {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> L_f</math>}} and {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> L_g</math>}} are equivalence classes of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \sim_A</math>}}.
Therefore, {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Sigma^\omega - L(A)</math>}} is an ω-regular language.
We can [[ω-regular language#Equivalence to Büchi automaton|translate the language]] into a Büchi automaton. This construction is doubly exponential in terms of size of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}}.
